title: Nutrition and metabolic support
summary: Nutrition and metabolic support in the ICU: nutritional risk and early enteral nutrition, energy and protein targets, feed intolerance, parenteral nutrition and refeeding syndrome, based on ESPEN 2019/2023 and ASPEN 2022.

topics.title: Nutritional risk and early enteral nutrition
topics.summary: Screen risk (mNUTRIC), start enteral feeding within 24-48 h when resuscitated, and know when to delay.

definition.text: Every ICU patient staying > 48 h is at risk of malnutrition. Early EN (within 48 h) is recommended over early PN or delayed EN when oral intake is not possible.

steps.title: Assess risk
steps.detail: mNUTRIC ≥ 5 (age, APACHE II, SOFA, comorbidities, days in hospital before ICU) or clinical malnutrition (weight loss, low BMI, sarcopenia, reduced intake) = high risk.

steps.title: Oral first
steps.detail: If able to eat, oral diet; add oral supplements if intake insufficient.

steps.title: Start EN within 48 h
steps.detail: Via nasogastric tube (confirm position by X-ray or pH); start low (10-20 mL/h) and advance over 3-7 days.

steps.title: Delay EN when
steps.detail: Uncontrolled shock, escalating vasopressors, uncontrolled life-threatening hypoxaemia or acidosis, active upper GI bleeding, overt bowel ischaemia, high-output fistula without distal access, abdominal compartment syndrome, GRV > 500 mL/6 h.

steps.title: Shock
steps.detail: Start low-dose (trophic) EN once shock controlled on stable or decreasing vasopressor doses; NUTRIREA-2 showed more bowel ischaemia with full early EN in shock.

steps.title: Prone, ECMO, TTM, NMB
steps.detail: EN is not contraindicated - continue at low dose with monitoring.

redFlags.text: Abdominal distension, rising lactate and vasopressor requirements on EN: suspect non-occlusive bowel ischaemia - stop feeds and investigate.

pitfalls.text: Keeping patients nil by mouth for days 'until stable' without a reason.
Blind tube placement without position confirmation.

pearls.text: Bowel sounds and flatus are not required to start EN.

nodes.text: Contraindication to EN (uncontrolled shock, ischaemia, GI bleed)?
Delay EN; reassess daily; consider PN if prolonged
Start NG EN at 10-20 mL/h within 48 h
Advance to 70% target by day 3-7; full later

consultantNotes.pathophysiology: Critical illness causes catabolism, insulin resistance and muscle wasting (up to 1 kg muscle/day in the first week). EN maintains gut barrier and immune function; early full feeding cannot suppress endogenous glucose production and may add to the energy load.
consultantNotes.evidence:
- ESPEN 2019/2023 and ASPEN 2022 guidelines [Singer 2019; Singer 2023; Compher 2022].
- NUTRIC/mNUTRIC risk tools [Heyland 2011; Rahman 2016].
- NUTRIREA-2: early full EN vs PN in shock - similar mortality, more GI complications with EN [Reignier 2018].
consultantNotes.controversies: - Value of risk scores to select who benefits; early EN in shock.
consultantNotes.indiaNotes:
- Many Indian ICUs use kitchen-prepared (blenderised) feeds because of cost; they have variable composition and higher contamination and tube-blockage risk - standardise recipes with dietitians.
- IL-6 is rarely available, so mNUTRIC is used.

topics.title: Energy and protein targets
topics.summary: Hypocaloric start (≤ 70% of expenditure) in the first days, advance to 80-100% after day 3, protein about 1.3 g/kg/day, adjust for obesity and count non-nutritional calories.

definition.text: Energy target is ideally measured by indirect calorimetry; otherwise use 20-25 kcal/kg/day in the early phase and 25-30 kcal/kg/day in recovery. Protein ~1.3 g/kg/day delivered progressively (ESPEN); ASPEN 1.2-2.0 g/kg/day.

steps.title: Weight
steps.detail: Use actual weight if BMI < 30; for obesity use adjusted or ideal body weight (see table).

steps.title: Early phase (days 1-3)
steps.detail: Hypocaloric: ≤ 70% of energy expenditure; avoid overfeeding.

steps.title: Later phase
steps.detail: After day 3 advance to 80-100% of measured or estimated energy expenditure.

steps.title: Protein
steps.detail: Target ~1.3 g/kg/day progressively; very high protein (≥ 2.2 g/kg) early did not improve outcomes and may harm patients with AKI or high organ failure scores (EFFORT Protein).

steps.title: Shock
steps.detail: In ventilated patients with shock, lower energy/protein in the first week (NUTRIREA-3) was associated with faster recovery and fewer complications.

steps.title: Count non-nutritional calories
steps.detail: Propofol 1.1 kcal/mL, dextrose 5% (~170 kcal/L), citrate in CRRT; reduce feed if large.

steps.title: Micronutrients and glucose
steps.detail: Provide micronutrients with feeding; insulin if glucose > 180 mg/dL (target about 140-180 mg/dL).

tables.title: Practical targets
rows: Add ~0.2 g/kg/day for losses (up to 1.5-1.7 g/kg)

redFlags.text: Hyperglycaemia, hypercapnia, rising urea and liver steatosis may indicate overfeeding.

pitfalls.text: Using actual weight for energy in morbid obesity.

pearls.text: VCO2 from the ventilator × 8.19 gives a reasonable estimate of energy expenditure when calorimetry is unavailable (ESPEN).

consultantNotes.pathophysiology: In the acute phase, endogenous glucose production (up to 50-75% of needs) cannot be suppressed by feeding, so full exogenous calories cause overfeeding; autophagy may be beneficial early. Anabolic potential increases in recovery.
consultantNotes.evidence:
- ESPEN 2019/2023: hypocaloric early, 1.3 g/kg protein progressively [Singer 2019; 2023].
- EFFORT Protein (1,329 patients): higher protein did not improve time to discharge alive; possible harm in AKI and high SOFA [Heyland 2023].
- NUTRIREA-3: low vs standard calories/protein in shock - similar mortality, faster readiness for discharge [Reignier 2023].
- TARGET: energy-dense EN (1.5 kcal/mL) did not improve survival [TARGET 2018].
consultantNotes.controversies: - Optimal protein dose and timing; indirect calorimetry for all.
consultantNotes.indiaNotes:
- Indian patients may have lower muscle mass ('thin-fat' phenotype) - assess muscle by ultrasound or clinical judgement; use IBW-based estimates for obesity.
- Vegetarian diets are common; commercial high-protein formulas or whey/soy protein supplements are used to meet targets.

topics.title: Feed intolerance, gastric residuals and post-pyloric feeding
topics.summary: Define intolerance, use a GRV threshold of 500 mL/6 h, give prokinetics, consider post-pyloric feeding and reduce aspiration risk.

definition.text: Feed intolerance: vomiting, GRV > 500 mL/6 h, distension, or diarrhoea preventing delivery of targets. Routine GRV monitoring is optional in ASPEN; ESPEN suggests delaying EN if GRV > 500 mL/6 h.

steps.title: Exclude serious causes
steps.detail: Bowel obstruction, ischaemia, ileus, raised IAP, electrolyte disturbance, opioids, hyperglycaemia.

steps.title: GRV > 500 mL/6 h
steps.detail: Pause or reduce feed rate, re-infuse up to 500 mL, start prokinetic.

steps.title: Prokinetics
steps.detail: Erythromycin 100-250 mg IV q8h (first choice) or metoclopramide 10 mg IV q8h, or both; review after 24-72 h.

steps.title: Post-pyloric feeding
steps.detail: If intolerance persists despite prokinetics, or high aspiration risk: nasojejunal tube (endoscopic, fluoroscopic or bedside electromagnetic).

steps.title: Aspiration prevention
steps.detail: Head-up 30-45°, continuous rather than bolus feeds, oral care, minimise sedation.

steps.title: Diarrhoea
steps.detail: Check C. difficile, laxatives, sorbitol-containing drugs, antibiotics; continue EN; consider soluble fibre or peptide formula.

redFlags.text: New distension with large GRVs, hypotension and lactate rise: stop EN and image the abdomen (bowel ischaemia/obstruction).

pitfalls.text: Stopping feeds for small GRVs (< 500 mL) - leads to underfeeding.
Long-term prokinetics (> 3-4 days): tachyphylaxis and side effects.

pearls.text: Diarrhoea is rarely due to the feed itself - look for drugs and infection first.

consultantNotes.pathophysiology: Critical illness impairs antral motility and gastric emptying (catecholamines, opioids, hyperglycaemia, electrolyte disorders, sepsis), while small bowel absorptive function is often preserved - the basis for post-pyloric feeding.
consultantNotes.evidence:
- ESPEN 2019: GRV 500 mL/6 h threshold; erythromycin first-line prokinetic; post-pyloric if persistent [Singer 2019].
- ASPEN 2022 guidance [Compher 2022].
consultantNotes.controversies: - Measuring GRV at all; combined prokinetics.
consultantNotes.indiaNotes: - Bedside NJ placement techniques (blind or electromagnetic) are less available in India; endoscopic placement by gastroenterology is the usual route.

topics.title: Parenteral nutrition
topics.summary: When to start PN (severe malnutrition early, others after day 3-7), how to prescribe and monitor, and complications.

definition.text: PN is indicated when EN is contraindicated or insufficient. ESPEN: in patients who cannot eat or be fed enterally, start PN within 3-7 days; in severe malnutrition start early, progressively. Supplemental PN can be considered when EN is < 60% of target after the first week.

steps.title: Decide timing
steps.detail: Well-nourished low-risk patients: delay PN (EPaNIC showed harm with early supplemental PN). Malnourished/high-risk with contraindication to EN: start PN early and advance slowly (refeeding precautions).

steps.title: Access
steps.detail: Dedicated lumen of a central venous catheter (or PICC) for standard PN; peripheral PN only for low-osmolarity short-term solutions (< 850-900 mOsm/L).

steps.title: Prescription
steps.detail: Use commercial 3-in-1 bags (glucose, amino acids, lipid) plus electrolytes, trace elements and vitamins; glucose ≤ 5 mg/kg/min; lipid ≤ 1.5 g/kg/day.

steps.title: Monitor
steps.detail: Glucose 4-6 hourly initially (insulin if > 180 mg/dL), electrolytes including phosphate and Mg daily at first, triglycerides (reduce lipid if > 400 mg/dL), LFT weekly.

steps.title: Complications
steps.detail: CLABSI (strict asepsis, dedicated lumen), hyperglycaemia, refeeding syndrome, PN-associated liver disease, overfeeding.

steps.title: Transition
steps.detail: Reduce PN as EN delivery reaches ~60-75% of target.

redFlags.text: Fever with PN running through a central line: suspect CLABSI - cultures from line and periphery; consider line removal.

pitfalls.text: Starting full-dose PN on day 1 in a well-nourished patient.
Adding lipid without accounting for propofol.

pearls.text: CALORIES: early PN was not more harmful than early EN when calories were matched - route matters less than avoiding overfeeding.

consultantNotes.pathophysiology: PN bypasses the gut, so there is no first-pass regulation of nutrient delivery; hyperglycaemia, infection and hepatic steatosis are more likely with excess dextrose and lipid.
consultantNotes.evidence:
- EPaNIC (4,640 patients): late PN (day 8) led to fewer infections and faster recovery than early supplemental PN [Casaer 2011].
- CALORIES (2,400): PN vs EN route - no mortality difference [Harvey 2014].
consultantNotes.controversies: - Supplemental PN timing in high-risk patients; lipid emulsion type (fish oil).
consultantNotes.indiaNotes:
- Commercial 3-in-1 PN bags are available in India but expensive; compounding pharmacies are limited to large hospitals.
- Strict CVC care bundles are essential given high CLABSI rates.

topics.title: Refeeding syndrome
topics.summary: Identify risk, start feeds low with thiamine, monitor phosphate, potassium and magnesium, and restrict calories if phosphate falls.

definition.text: Refeeding syndrome: electrolyte shifts (hypophosphataemia, hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia) and thiamine deficiency after starting nutrition in a starved patient, causing organ dysfunction (respiratory failure, arrhythmia, heart failure, delirium) usually within 72 h (ASPEN: fall in phosphate, K or Mg by 10-20% mild, 20-30% moderate, > 30% or organ dysfunction severe).

steps.title: Identify risk
steps.detail: BMI < 16-18.5, weight loss > 5-15% in 1-6 months, little or no intake for > 5-10 days, low K/PO4/Mg before feeding, alcohol use disorder, chronic illness, cancer, eating disorders.

steps.title: Thiamine first
steps.detail: Thiamine 100 mg before feeding and daily for 5-7 days.

steps.title: Start low
steps.detail: 10-20 kcal/kg for first 24 h, advance by 33% of goal every 1-2 days; correct electrolytes before and during (do not delay feeding solely to correct them).

steps.title: Monitor
steps.detail: Phosphate, K, Mg every 12 h for 3 days in high-risk patients, then daily; fluid balance, heart rate, glucose.

steps.title: If phosphate falls
steps.detail: Phosphate < 2 mg/dL (0.65 mmol/L) or falls > 30% after starting feeds: reduce energy intake (REFEED: restrict to ~20 kcal/h for 2 days, then increase gradually) and replace phosphate.

steps.title: Replace
steps.detail: IV phosphate 0.16-0.64 mmol/kg depending on severity; K and Mg as needed.

doseCards.dose: 100 mg before feeds, then daily for 5-7 days

doseCards.workedExample: 70 kg: 11-22 mmol phosphate in 250 mL NS over 6 h

redFlags.text: New respiratory muscle weakness, failed weaning, arrhythmia or confusion 2-3 days after starting feeds: check phosphate.

pitfalls.text: Starting full feeds in a starved alcoholic patient without thiamine and electrolyte monitoring.

pearls.text: Hypophosphataemia in ventilated patients delays weaning and impairs diaphragm function - check phosphate before SBTs.

consultantNotes.pathophysiology: Feeding after starvation triggers insulin release and anabolism; phosphate, potassium and magnesium move intracellularly and are consumed in ATP and glycogen synthesis, and thiamine is used in carbohydrate metabolism - causing acute deficiency states.
consultantNotes.evidence:
- ASPEN 2020 consensus definitions and management [da Silva 2020].
- REFEED: caloric restriction in refeeding hypophosphataemia improved survival [Doig 2015].
consultantNotes.controversies: - Diagnostic criteria; the degree of initial caloric restriction needed.
consultantNotes.indiaNotes: - Undernutrition, tuberculosis, alcohol use and prolonged illness before referral are common in Indian ICU patients - refeeding risk is high; ensure phosphate testing is available.

drugs.name: Erythromycin
drugs.indications: Gastric feed intolerance (first choice in ESPEN)
drugs.adultDose: 100-250 mg IV every 8 h for 24-72 h (tachyphylaxis after ~3 days).
drugs.verify: IV erythromycin availability in India; oral suspension sometimes substituted.

drugs.name: Metoclopramide
drugs.adultDose: 10 mg IV every 8 h; review after 3 days.

drugs.name: Thiamine
drugs.indications: Refeeding risk; alcohol use; prolonged starvation
drugs.adultDose: 100 mg (oral/IV) before starting feeds and daily for 5-7 days (or longer in severe starvation/alcohol use).

drugs.name: Phosphate replacement (potassium or sodium phosphate)
drugs.adultDose: Moderate (1.0-1.9 mg/dL): 0.16-0.32 mmol/kg IV over 4-6 h; severe (< 1.0 mg/dL): 0.32-0.64 mmol/kg IV over 8-12 h (max ~50 mmol per dose); oral phosphate for mild deficits.
drugs.renalHepatic: Reduce doses in AKI; monitor closely.
drugs.cautions: Potassium phosphate adds potassium (check K); hypocalcaemia with rapid infusion.
drugs.verify: Local preparation (mmol phosphate per mL) and replacement protocol.
